item.title: The Complete Dictionary
item.description:
This is the capstone post of the series. It does not prove new results. It collects the complete translation between linear algebra and its categorification, states the series thesis precisely, and notes what the categorical version adds beyond the classical one.

The dictionary

Linear algebra Categorified linear algebra
Vector $v \in V$ Object $M \in \mathcal{A}$
Vector space $V$ $k$-linear category $\mathcal{A}$
Linear operator $T : V \to V$ Endofunctor $S : \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{A}$
Action $Tv$ Image $S(M)$
Eigenvalue equation $Tv = \mu v$ Structure map $s_M : M \to S(M)$
Eigenvalue $\mu \in k$ Natural transformation $\lambda : \operatorname{id}_{\mathcal{A}} \Rightarrow S$
Canonical eigenvector Canonical $\lambda$-eigenobject $(M, \lambda_M)$
Eigenspace $E_\mu(T)$ Category $\operatorname{Eig}_\lambda(S) \subseteq \operatorname{Rep}(S)$
Krylov sequence $v, Tv, T^2v, \ldots$ Orbit tower $M \to S(M) \to S^2(M) \to \cdots$
Commuting operators $ST = TS$ Commutation datum $\alpha : ST \xRightarrow{\sim} TS$
Preservation $T(E_\mu(S)) \subseteq E_\mu(S)$ $\widetilde{T}$ preserves $\operatorname{Eig}_\lambda(S)$
Compatibility condition $\alpha_M^{-1} \circ T(\lambda_M) = \lambda_{T(M)}$
Invariant flag Filtration $\mathcal{A}_0 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq \mathcal{A}_n = \mathcal{A}$
Triangularization Preservation of filtration with canonical quotient eigendata
Diagonalization Decomposition $\mathcal{A} \simeq \bigoplus_\beta \mathcal{A}_\beta$ into stable eigenblocks
Linear functional $V \to k$ $k$-linear functor $F : \mathcal{A} \to \operatorname{Vect}_k$
Dual space $V^*$ $\mathcal{A}^* = \operatorname{Fun}_k(\mathcal{A}, \operatorname{Vect}_k)$
Transpose $L^* : W^* \to V^*$ Precomposition: $L^*(F) = F \circ L$
Double dual $V^{**}$ $\mathcal{A}^{**} = \operatorname{Fun}_k(\mathcal{A}^*, \operatorname{Vect}_k)$
Reflexivity $V \cong V^{**}$ Equivalence $J_{\mathcal{A}} : \mathcal{A} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{A}^{**}$ (a condition, not automatic)
Eigenvector of $T^*$ Canonical $\lambda^*$-eigenfunctional $(F, F(\lambda))$
Polynomial coefficient $a_i \in k$ Coefficient vector space $V_i$
Polynomial in $T$ $P(S) = \bigoplus_i V_i \otimes S^i$
Polynomial multiplication (Cauchy) $P(S) \circ Q(S) \cong \bigoplus_n \left(\bigoplus_{i+j=n} V_i \otimes W_j\right) \otimes S^n$
Polynomial relation $p(T) = 0$ Natural transformation $P(S) \Rightarrow 0$
Annihilator ideal in $k[x]$ $\operatorname{Ann}_{k[x]}([M])$ in $K_0(\mathcal{A})$
Linear factor $x - \mu$ Linear factor datum $\lambda : \operatorname{id} \Rightarrow S$
Generalized eigenspace $(T - \mu)^n v = 0$ Generalized $\lambda$-relation of rank $n$
Polynomial factorization $p = qr$ Factorization datum $P(S) \cong Q(S) \circ R(S)$

What the categorified version adds

The dictionary above might suggest that categorification is a straightforward substitution. It is not. Three features of the categorical theory have no classical counterpart.

item.title: Linear Factors, Generalized Eigenobjects, and Factorization
item.description:
In ordinary linear algebra over an algebraically closed field, the minimal polynomial of an operator $T$ factors completely into linear factors $(x - \mu_i)^{n_i}$. The eigenvalue $\mu_i$ gives the degree-one part; the power $n_i$ encodes the Jordan block structure. This post identifies the categorical analogues of both.

Linear factor data

The natural transformation $\lambda : \operatorname{id}_{\mathcal{A}} \Rightarrow S$ is a linear factor datum.

The term is chosen deliberately. In the polynomial $x - \mu$, the scalar $\mu$ gives a specific map from the identity operator to $T$: it is the datum $v \mapsto \mu v$. The natural transformation $\lambda$ plays the same role: it gives a specific map from the identity functor to $S$, one component per object.

item.title: Polynomial Relations and Annihilator Ideals
item.description: In ordinary linear algebra, the minimal polynomial of a vector $v$ with respect to an operator $T$ is the monic polynomial $p$ of least degree such that $p(T)v = 0$. The equation $p(T)v = 0$ is a statement about an element of a vector space. Categorically, neither “element” nor “zero” transfers directly. The correct replacement involves natural transformations, and the classical ideal theory emerges only after passing to a decategorified shadow.

item.title: Categorified Polynomials and the Cauchy Product
item.description:
Given a linear operator $T : V \to V$, ordinary linear algebra studies expressions of the form

$$p(T) = a_0 \operatorname{id} + a_1 T + \cdots + a_n T^n, \qquad a_i \in k.$$

These are polynomials in $T$ with scalar coefficients. The minimal polynomial is the lowest-degree $p$ such that $p(T) = 0$. For a categorified endofunctor $S$, the powers $S^i$ still make sense. But the scalar coefficient $a_i \in k$ does not: there is no canonical way to attach a scalar to a functor.

item.title: The Same Compatibility Equation on Both Sides
item.description:
Post IV established that the lifted functor $\widetilde{T}$ preserves canonical $\lambda$-eigenobjects if and only if

$$\alpha_M^{-1} \circ T(\lambda_M) = \lambda_{T(M)}$$

for every object $M$. This is the central compatibility equation of the object side.

Now transpose everything. The commutation datum $\alpha : ST \Rightarrow TS$ transposes to a natural isomorphism $\alpha^* : T^* S^* \Rightarrow S^* T^*$. The lifted functor $T^*$ acts on $\mathcal{A}^*$, and the question is: when does $T^*$ preserve canonical $\lambda^*$-eigenfunctionals?

item.title: Double Duals and Eigenfunctionals
item.description:
The previous post defined the canonical functor $J_{\mathcal{A}} : \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{A}^{**}$ by $J_{\mathcal{A}}(M)(F) = F(M)$. For a finite-dimensional vector space $V$, the analogous map $V \to V^{**}$ is an isomorphism. The categorical version need not be an equivalence, and the failure of reflexivity is a meaningful geometric and algebraic datum, not a defect of the definition.

Reflexivity as a condition

Definition. A $k$-linear category $\mathcal{A}$ is reflexive if $J_{\mathcal{A}} : \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{A}^{**}$ is an equivalence of categories.

item.title: Categorified Functionals and Transpose
item.description:
The first half of this series established the object side of categorified linear algebra: representations, eigenobjects, orbit towers, commuting endofunctors, and filtrations. The second half develops the functional side. The organizing question is: if a $k$-linear category plays the role of a vector space, what plays the role of a linear functional?

Categorified functionals

A linear functional on a vector space $V$ is a linear map $V \to k$. Replacing $V$ by a $k$-linear category $\mathcal{A}$ and $k$ by the category of $k$-vector spaces, the direct analogue is a $k$-linear functor

item.title: Triangularization and Diagonalization Without Matrices
item.description:
Simultaneous triangularization in linear algebra says that a commuting family of operators can sometimes be put into upper-triangular form with respect to a common basis. But the basis is not the point. The basis is a way of representing a flag: a chain of invariant subspaces

$$0 = V_0 \subsetneq V_1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq V_n = V,$$

each stable under every operator in the family. The matrix is upper-triangular because the flag is invariant; the flag is the real structure.

item.title: Commuting Endofunctors and Preservation of Eigenspaces
item.description:
If two operators on a vector space commute, $ST = TS$, then $T$ maps each eigenspace of $S$ into itself. The proof is one line: if $Sv = \mu v$ and $ST = TS$, then $S(Tv) = T(Sv) = T(\mu v) = \mu(Tv)$.

The categorical analogue of this result requires more care, because strict equality $ST = TS$ of functors is almost never the right condition. Two functors that agree on every object and every morphism are equal, but in practice one works with functors that are isomorphic, not literally equal. The correct replacement for the equation $ST = TS$ is a specified natural isomorphism $\alpha : ST \xRightarrow{\sim} TS$.

item.title: Orbit Towers and Iterated Eigenmaps
item.description:
Given a linear operator $T : V \to V$ and a vector $v \in V$, one forms the Krylov sequence

$$v,\quad Tv,\quad T^2v,\quad T^3v,\quad \ldots$$

All of these live in $V$. The sequence is the raw material for cyclic subspaces, minimal polynomials, and Jordan theory.

For an endofunctor $S : \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{A}$, the analogous construction is not a sequence of objects inside one ambient category (they already all live in $\mathcal{A}$) but a sequence of maps connecting successive iterates. The maps are the content; the objects alone do not determine them.

item.title: Eigenvalues as Natural Transformations
item.description: The previous post introduced $\operatorname{Rep}(S)$: the category of objects equipped with a chosen structure map $s_M : M \to S(M)$. Any morphism $M \to S(M)$ qualifies, so $\operatorname{Rep}(S)$ is large and undifferentiated. The linear algebraic eigenvalue equation $Tv = \mu v$ is more specific: the scalar $\mu$ determines the action on all vectors simultaneously, not just on one chosen vector. The categorical analogue of this specificity is a natural transformation.

item.title: From Operators to Endofunctors
item.description: A linear operator $T : V \to V$ acts on vectors inside one fixed ambient space. The equation $Tv = \mu v$ makes sense because both sides live in $V$. Once that ambient space is replaced by a category, this sentence stops parsing. The left side $S(M)$ is an object produced by a functor; the right side $\mu \cdot M$ has no meaning without scalar multiplication on objects. The right response is not to force the equation to make sense. It is to find the structure that the equation was secretly encoding.

item.title: Vertex-Wise Linear Algebra
item.description:
If you have ever taken a linear algebra course, you likely spent a significant amount of time analyzing square matrices. You calculated determinants, found eigenvalues, and perhaps wrestled with the Jordan Normal Form.

Later, you might have realized that a matrix is essentially a coordinate-dependent projection of a more fundamental object: a linear map between vector spaces. A matrix is what we obtain when we fix a basis.

But there is a third perspective. This approach takes the “vector space and map” intuition and lifts it into a combinatorial setting. This perspective allows us to perform linear algebra not just locally at a single node, but across a network. This is the theory of Quiver Representations.
